Common free bet traps
Below, we’ve provided some detail on common traps that users can fall into when claiming free bets:
Stake not returned on free bets
Most free bet offers do not return the stake if your bet wins. For example, a £10 free bet at 3/1 pays £30 profit, not £40; always factor this in when using your free bet tokens.
Short expiry windows
Free bets usually expire within 5-7 days of being credited, and occasionally less. Unused free bets are removed automatically once they expire, so casual or infrequent bettors can lose value this way.
Remember to always check the expiry date as soon as the free bet is added.
Bet builder or market restrictions

Bet builder-only free bets often require multiple selections to win, meaning long odds, and it is the same with accas. Remember to check eligible markets before placing your qualifying bet.
Minimum odds requirements
Betting offers may require minimum odds on either the qualifying bet or the free bet itself, and sometimes both. Higher odds thresholds can push bettors toward riskier selections, while a smaller free bet with low odds requirements can offer better value.
Cash-Out and In-Play exclusions
Remember that cashing out a qualifying bet often voids eligibility for the offer. Some free bets also cannot be used on in-play markets.
These exclusions are commonly hidden in the T&Cs, so avoid cashing out unless you’re sure it won’t affect the promotion.
Wagering requirements and bonus conditions
Wagering is uncommon on free bets, but it is not unheard of. Some promotions attach extra conditions to winnings or follow-on bonuses instead.
Betting offers requiring winnings to be wagered multiple times reduce real value, while simpler “bet and get” free bets are usually the safest option.

title: Minister urges Britons to stock up on food and water after El Nino extreme weather warning
text:
Minister urges Britons to stock up on food and water after El Nino extreme weather warning
Forecasters predict the biggest El Nino in 1,000 years which is set to bring and wet and stormy winter to the UK
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Britons have been urged to stock up on enough food and water to survive a few days without power or a water supply.
It comes as forecasters predict the biggest El Nino in 1,000 years, which could bring extreme heat, flooding and wildfires across the globe. The UK is likely to be hit with a wet and stormy winter.
The government is planning a campaign to advise citizens to prepare for national emergencies and Environment Secretary Angela Eagle stressed the importance of keeping supplies at home.
Speaking about the wetter winters and drier summers the El Nino will bring, Ms Eagle told the Guardian: “It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.
“If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t. So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient.”
El Nino is a meteorological phenomenon where sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean get warmer.
It usually occurs every two to seven years and lasts several months disrupting weather patterns worldwide and pushing up global temperatures.
Forecasts from the the World Meteorological Organisation’s (WMO) global network of climate centres expects the El Nino to peak towards the end of this year, with impacts from the weather phenomenon likely to continue well into next year.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific, WMO secretary-General Celeste Saulo warned it has “the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world”.
Analysis from the Energy and Climate Unit (ECIU) found that countries that could be exposed to climate extremes were the source of 13 per cent of UK food imports.
That means food such as rice, for which India is the UKs biggest supplier and citrus fruits from South Africa and Peru, coffee from Brazil and tea from Kenya could all be impacted.
The threat of hot weather and storms comes after five back-to-back heatwaves plunged the country into drought. This has already put severe pressure on the water system, wildlife, farmers, emergency services and infrastructure.
Tinned food and bottled water are some of the essential items a campaign from the Cabinet Office could ask people to stock up on in the coming months.
Meanwhile Ms Eagle is set to oversee farming improvements and a new programme of reservoir building to prepare the countries for future years where extreme weather is more likely.

title: What drove the deadly Grand Canyon flooding?
text:
What drove the deadly Grand Canyon flooding?
Torrential downpours washed out popular hiking trails and left the historic Phantom Ranch Lodge cabins under five feet of water
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
At least two people are dead and 15 others still missing in Arizona’s Grand Canyon National Park after flash flooding from a storm that dropped nearly an inch of rain per hour this weekend.
Torrential downpours lasted for three hours Saturday afternoon, washing out popular hiking trails and leaving the historic Phantom Ranch Lodge cabins in the Bright Angel Canyon area under five feet of water.
The rains overwhelmed areas already saturated by downpours from earlier that day. It resulted in debris flows that took many park-goers by surprise and led to helicopter rescues for more than 60 people.
The search for the missing continues. The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River Sunday night, and at least one other body has been recovered, according to a Monday statement by the park. Neither of the deceased individuals have been identified.
“I don’t think we would have made it out alive if we had fallen into the creek and then we’d gotten carried into the Colorado River,” hiker David Gregory told CBS. “There was, like, a whirlpool in there.”
Another hiker, physician Parth Desai, said he was heading through a narrow passage when the rain started.
“We saw the creek flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere,” he said.
What is the forecast?
The Bright Angel Canyon area remains closed as the risk of flash flooding, debris flows, rockfalls and changing trail and river conditions continues Monday. The National Weather Service has a flood watch in place through Monday evening for northern and central Arizona.
“Additional scattered thunderstorms today across the Southwest, including northern Arizona into central Utah, will likely produce intense rainfall rates above 1” per hour,” the National Weather Service said in a post on X.
The deluge also seriously damaged the only water pipeline in the canyon. It has led to water restrictions for local communities, and hotel accommodations in the area are closed starting Monday night.
“The waterline is currently not operational, leaving the park with limited water reserves and requiring significant water conservation measures to ensure available supplies can be maintained,” the National Park Service said.
Grand Canyon National Park remains open for daytime visitors, though visitors are asked to remain out of the closure area while search and rescue operations continue.
What caused the flooding?
Monsoon rains, driven by shifting winds, are a typical feature in the region during the warm summer months. So are flash floods, which killed four people last September in Arizona’s eastern-central Gila County.
But dangerous flooding is also part of the larger story of a super El Niño climate pattern that has developed this summer.
El Niño occurs when winds shift over the Pacific Ocean, allowing warm water to flow eastward. This change often brings wetter weather to the American Southwest.
El Niño’s effects combined with a marine heat wave, worsened by human-caused climate change, helped contribute to the flooding, according to The Washington Post’s meteorologist Ben Knoll.
A hotter ocean helps create a warmer atmosphere, which is able to hold more moisture, and is driving hurricane formation on the West Coast.
“On the backdrop of climate change, these factors have driven atmospheric moisture levels 5 to 15 percent higher than average. That has loaded the dice for downpours this summer, such as those that hit the Grand Canyon on Saturday,” he explained.
This summer is expected to be one of the warmest - if not the warmest - on record. July was the hottest July ever and August has already seen heat records broken.
But wasn’t there a drought?
The disastrous flooding follows America’s worst-ever spring drought.
Heavy rain on drought-ravaged land increases the risk of flash flooding events because it’s harder for the baked earth to absorb the water.
Arizona is currently less drought-riddled than a lot of the West, but the federal U.S. Drought Monitor shows most of the state is still in moderate-to-severe drought.
The Bright Angel Canyon area gets around 10 inches of rainfall a year on average, the National Park Service says.
The National Park Service has asked anyone with information about people who are unaccounted for to come forward. They can contact the NPS Investigative Services Branch Tip Line at 888-653-0009.

title: Anguish for families as no missing Britons among the hundreds rescued after Nepal flash floods
text:
Anguish for families as no missing Britons among the hundreds rescued after Nepal flash floods
Nepal’s tourist board issued an update on almost 300 people rescued so far as further warnings were issued with water levels rising again
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
None of the 33 British citizens reported missing in Nepal after devastating flash floods have been rescued, authorities said on Sunday.
More than 700 people have died with more than 3,000 reported missing after disaster struck following the collapse of a glacier on Wednesday. Authorities have warned of a further risk of flooding as water levels rose along the Bhotekoshi River and urged residents to remain on high alert.
Hundreds of those unaccounted for are foreign nationals including 33 previously reported missing by authorities on the Nepal side of the border. Chinese authorities have also reported 15 Britons missing in Tibet, although its unclear if they are included in Nepal’s figures.
In an update on Sunday night, Nepal’s tourism board said at least 289 people had been rescued so far, but the breakdown of nationalities showed no British people listed among them.
“Search, rescue, evacuation and assistance operations are continuing for those who remain stranded, injured or otherwise affected” the Nepal Tourism Board said.
Among the rescued nationalities are 180 Indian citizens, 89 Chinese, and several individuals from Europe including one person from Bulgaria and Portugal and two Americans.
Pramod Poudel, 34, a food truck owner from East Sussex, told The Sun that his wife, mother, brother and uncle remain missing. He flew out to Nepal to help find them on Friday.
“When I last spoke to her, she said to me, ‘How are you? I love you so much’,” he said.
“I have not had contact with her since then. It’s devastating — I don’t even know how to explain how I’m feeling right now. I’m so worried about her, and all my family. I work so hard for them and they are my whole world. I’m very hopeful of finding them but I’m also praying to God.”
Beijing said missing foreign nationals represented 23 nationalities, while Nepal previously listed people from 33 countries among more than 500 foreign nationals unaccounted for.
Heat and humidity mean that many of the recovered bodies have decomposed beyond recognition.
“Many have no visible faces,” police officer Anil Thapa told Reuters. “In some cases, only hands or legs remain; in others, only parts of the body are available.”
At least 96 unidentified bodies were buried on Saturday with plans to bury over 100 more on Sunday, authorities said. DNA samples were collected in the hope that relatives would be able to identify their loved ones at a later date.
Around 350 people are also reported to be trapped inside a tunnel in a hydropower project as operations to reach them continued on Sunday. ,
Around 10,000 Nepali troops have been deployed to assist with the disaster alongside specialist teams from China and India. The Red Cross estimates that more than 90,000 people have been impacted across the region.
Nepalese officials said bridges have been destroyed and nearly 25 miles of roads have been damaged, which has complicated search efforts.
On Saturday, a rapid deployment team from the UK arrived in Nepal to provide support for Britons and their families.

What triggered Nepal flash floods? And why are experts worried a second flood is ‘imminent’?
Signal detected by monitors for seismic activity actually came from the force of ‘glacial collapse and debris flow’
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The Himalayan flash floods that killed at least 768 people and left over 3,000 missing across Nepal and Tibet were not triggered by an earthquake, contrary to initial reports, but by a glacier collapse so violent that it produced its own seismic signal, the United States Geological Survey said.
The agency initially recorded a magnitude 4.4 earthquake along the Nepal-China border, north of Kathmandu, at about 8.37am local time on Wednesday, before revising its assessment in a statement issued that evening.
It said the seismic signal had come from “a glacial collapse and debris flow” rather than a tectonic quake, and that the collapse alone had caused the catastrophic flooding downstream. Once reclassified, the event registered at magnitude 5.2, a measure of the force of the ice and rock striking the valley floor rather than of any movement underground.
An initial study of satellite imagery from Planet Labs showed a large section of the lower end of a glacier breaking away at an altitude of about 5,200m and falling roughly 1,200m onto the valley floor, gathering rock and debris as it went.
The resulting avalanche struck the Lhende river in Tibet, about 20km northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing with Nepal, temporarily damming the water before the barrier gave way and released a powerful flood downstream.
The surge fed into the Bhote Koshi river and crossed into Nepal at around 9am local time, then continued into the Trishuli river, where water levels rose by as much as nine metres in just half an hour.
Officials were caught off guard because there had been no rain, according to local news reports, and some residents ignored early warnings from neighbours precisely because the danger did not resemble the monsoon flooding they were used to.
Nepal’s Rasuwa district, immediately south of the border, bore the worst of the damage, with the flood also reaching Nuwakot and Dhading further downstream. At least 19 bridges and around 40km of roads were destroyed, and damaged hydropower infrastructure left some areas without electricity.
Adrian McCallum, a glaciologist and polar engineer at the University of the Sunshine Coast, said the disaster had the hallmarks of a glacial lake outburst flood. “As glaciers melt and recede, ice turns to water, the water is stored behind natural moraine dams, but when those dams breach, tremendous amounts of water can be released down a valley, taking out everything in its path,” he explained.
Ruth Gamble, environmental historian and director of La Trobe Asia at La Trobe University, said that the flood behaved “like an inland tsunami”, travelling 170km down the Bhote Koshi valley into central Nepal, along a route also used by tourists travelling between Kathmandu and Lhasa.
Why are experts worried a second flood is coming?
Both Nepal and China have issued warnings about fresh flooding in the Himalayas as two lakes that have developed on either side of their border threaten to burst.
Experts were assessing whether debris from the flood had temporarily blocked Nepal's Trishuli river at a narrow section, forming a landslide dam, the Nepal-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said.
Such a blockage can create a secondary hazard if impounded water is suddenly released.
“With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border, authorities warn a second flood is imminent,” Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at ICIMOD, said.
He added that evacuation orders were in place for Jilong Port along the border based on the risk of a second wave of flooding.
China warned that 3 million cubic meters of water — the equivalent of about 1,200 Olympic swimming pools — was expected to flow into an already dammed lake on its side of the border over the next three days, creating a high risk of a breach, with peak flow expected around September 1.
Rainfall forecast over the coming week could exacerbate the threat, Chinese state media said, citing the water resources ministry.
"The volume of water is continuing to increase, and so is the risk," Zhu Jinfeng, a researcher at the water resources ministry's hydrology department, told CCTV.
Scientists cautioned it was too early to say how much climate change contributed to the collapse itself. Glaciers across the wider Hindu Kush Himalaya region, spanning Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar and Bangladesh, lost ice 65 per cent faster between 2011 and 2020 than in the previous decade. Nepal’s own glaciers have lost about a third of their ice volume over roughly the past three decades.
Satellite observations showed unusually warm conditions and reduced snow cover around the glacier before it collapsed, exposing more bare ice, though researchers were yet to determine a direct link to this week’s disaster.
Nader Naderpajouh, head of the school of project management at the University of Sydney, said the disaster could prompt the introduction of early warning systems similar to those developed after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, since a water build-up behind a glacial dam could sometimes be detected before it burst.
“Such communications and preparations can save lives and reduce the impact at scale,” he said.

People across the UK have been urged to prepare an “emergency kit” as flooding and thunderstorms are expected to hit large areas of the country.
A yellow weather warning for thunderstorms is in force across huge swathes of England and Wales on Thursday as heavy rain batters the UK.
The Met Office has issued an urgent warning encouraging people to consider whether their homes are at risk of flooding, and if so, to prepare a flood plan and emergency supplies ahead of potential disruption.
It advises those in at-risk areas to prepare a bag including insurance documents and a list of contact numbers, a torch and spare batteries, a first aid kit and any prescription medicines, warm waterproof clothes and blankets, bottled water and snacks, a battery-powered or wind-up radio, and supplies for looking after a baby or pet if needed.
A band of thunderstorms and heavy rain is expected to move north across England and Wales throughout the day, dropping up to 50mm of rain across a 12-hour period in some places.
Parts of the West Midlands have already been hit by flooding following a warning for the Perry Barr district on Wednesday night, brought on by swelling river levels.
Forecasters have issued a yellow warning covering the East of England, East Midlands, West Midlands, London and south-east England, north-west England, south-west England, Yorkshire and the Humber, and Wales from 5am until 10pm on Thursday.
A total of 81 areas are covered by the warning.
A second warning covering parts of the East Midlands, east of England, London and south-east England, and Yorkshire and the Humber, is also in place from 5pm on Thursday to 7am on Friday.
The Environment Agency has issued one flood warning, meaning flooding is expected, and 39 flood alerts, meaning flooding is possible, across England.
Forecasters have warned of potential disruption and said there is a “small chance” of flooding impacting homes and businesses and posing a risk to life. Public transport and infrastructure could be affected by the conditions, with drivers urged to watch out for spray and sudden flooding on the roads.
The South East warning area could see 30 to 40mm of rainfall and “fairly large hail between 1 to 2cm”, while the bigger warning area could have more than 75mm of rain through 12 hours in parts, Met Office forecaster Craig Snell said.
Temperatures will drop closer to average for the time of the year over the weekend, with highs of 24 or 25C on Friday, then 22 or 23C until Monday.
Mr Snell added: “We’re watching the risk of some heavy rain and thunderstorms moving up from the south.
“On Thursday as we wake up there will be a band of potentially heavy rain and thundery rain stretching across parts of the UK.
“For parts of the Midlands and Wales it’s going to be quite a wet day really. We could see some further thunderstorms move into the south east around Thursday evening.”
Friday will see further heavy rain and thunderstorms across the UK, before further rain moves in on Saturday, and a mix of sunshine and showers on Sunday and Monday.
Mr Snell said: “To sum up the bank holiday weekend, it’s going to be pretty unsettled; there will be some sunny moments in between if you can dodge the downpours.

title: China reeling under floods triggered by Typhoon Narra as Saudel approaches Japan and Taiwan
text:
China reeling under floods triggered by Typhoon Narra as Saudel approaches Japan and Taiwan
Authorities in Chongzuo, in China's Guangxi region famous for its giant waterfalls and karst limestone mountains, evacuated more than 15,000 people
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Widespread floods triggered by heavy rain from Typhoon Narra intensified on Tuesday across southern China, with homes and shops submerged and thousands of people relocated, while another storm system made its way towards Japan and Taiwan.
Authorities in Chongzuo, in China's Guangxi region famous for its giant waterfalls and karst limestone mountains, evacuated more than 15,000 people after water levels surpassed a record high set in 2008.
Meanwhile, medium-strength Typhoon Saudel moved towards southern Japan and northern Taiwan where it is expected to bring sporadic heavy rain, as Taiwan reported one dead and four missing from a separate weather system over its south and east.
Rising floodwaters have prompted China to relocate a total of 54,000 people in Guangxi, state television said.
Narra has lingered over the Beibu Gulf, also known as the Gulf of Tonkin, in the northwestern part of the South China Sea for several days, dumping heavy rain on Guangxi and the nearby provinces of Hainan and Guangdong.
Heavy rain is expected to persist across parts of Vietnam and southern China through Wednesday, with areas of Guangxi, Guangdong, Hainan and Fujian forecast to receive torrential rain, state media said.
In Chongzuo, river water overflowed into the city, with water levels reaching the rooftops of some buildings and power lines.
A notice from Chongzuo authorities on Monday ordered all businesses and tourist operations to cease and urged evacuated residents not to return to high-risk areas.Japan's weather agency warned of destructive gusts as Typhoon Saudel approached the southwestern islands of Okinawa prefecture, also causing extremely strong winds and high seas.
Saudel is expected to pass to the north of Taiwan and dump water on its north starting late Thursday and into Friday, though its intensity is forecast to gradually weaken and its storm-force wind radius to shrink, the island's Central Weather Administration said.
However, there is uncertainty about the timing and extent of the typhoon's rainfall impact, it added.
In southern and eastern Taiwan, the government reported one person dead and four missing from a tropical depression that brought flooding in the cities of Tainan and Kaohsiung, home to more than four million people.
During the three days from Sunday to Tuesday, almost a metre (3.9ft) of rain fell in Kaohsiung, which the government said exceeded rainfall during 2009's devastating Typhoon Morakot that killed about 700 people and caused damage of up to $3bn.
Saudel is forecast to hit the coast in the southeastern Chinese province of Fujian from late Thursday to early Friday.

title: Crisis in Indiana after Gary residents left without power and water 2 weeks after storm
text:
Crisis in Indiana after Gary residents left without power and water 2 weeks after storm
The area’s electrical provider estimates most of its customers will have their power restored by Tuesday night
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Nearly 12,000 people in northwest Indiana were still without power Monday, nearly two weeks after deadly storms wrecked the region, downing trees and power lines.
Severe storms and flooding swept across the state on August 11, leaving over 374,500 without power at its peak.
The storm impacted hundreds of structures, triggered water rescues and left at least seven people dead, while many others were left in desperate need of food and water, the Indiana State Emergency Operations Center said.
The crisis persisted Monday, as over 11,800 outages were still ongoing in Lake County, Porter County and Randolph County.
Residents in Munster, Portage, Hammond, Lake Station and Merrillville all remained without power — although two-thirds of the remaining outages were in Gary, on the southern shore of Lake Michigan.
The area’s electrical provider, Northern Indiana Public Service Company, says it estimates power will be restored to Munster by 11:59 p.m. Monday, while Gary and Portage should see it restored by 11:59 p.m. Tuesday.
However, the estimates “should not be interpreted as the exact restoration time for an individual home or business,” the company warned.
The town of Gary was hit particularly hard by the storm, which the National Weather Service preliminarily identified as a derecho — or fast-moving bands of thunderstorms often referred to as “inland hurricanes.” These storms most frequently occur from May to August.
The service said it wouldn’t have a firm analysis on the storm until next year.
The derecho saw wind gusts in Gary peak at 99 mph, according to the National Weather Service.
Days later, residents still report damage and debris in the streets — and many even remain under a boil advisory for water. Even without electricity, students in Gary returned to school on Monday, with the district operating on a two-hour delay.
Gary Mayor Eddie Melton said that while the power company was making progress, it was still “unacceptable” that thousands of residents in the city are still without power nearly two weeks after the storm wreaked havoc on the region.
“We’re at day 12, and 12 days is too long for families to be without power,” Melton said in a video address shared online Sunday.
“Twelve days is too long for parents to worry about their children, and for businesses to lose revenue, and for families to wonder when the relief is finally going to come. Today, I want the people of Gary to know this. I want you to know that I share their frustration.”
Indiana Gov. Mike Braun announced Sunday that he was deploying the Indiana National Guard to help clear the way for power crews. Additionally, the power company ComEd sent dozens of crews to help restoration efforts.
On Monday, Braun wrote on X that he was calling for an investigation into Northern Indiana Public Service Company over the prolonged power outages.
“NIPSCO is a monopoly utility that Hoosiers pay every month with the expectation that it will use its considerable resources to maintain its system, prepare for severe weather and restore service as quickly as possible when disaster strikes. NIPSCO has failed to keep its end of the bargain,” Braun wrote.
NIPSCO predicts most of its customers will have their power restored by Tuesday night — a full two weeks after the devastating storm.
The Independent has contacted NIPSCO for comment.

title: How a record super El Nino could reshape extreme weather for 12 of Asiaâs biggest cities
text:
How an ‘unprecedented’ super El Nino could reshape extreme weather for 12 of Asia’s biggest cities
Exclusive: Cities could swing to opposite extremes – according to research from WaterAid – with some pushed towards drought and others facing flooding. Stuti Mishra reports
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Some of Asia's largest cities are likely to face months of drought while others could be hit by flooding when a “super” El Niño weather event develops later this year, according to research that warns it has no precedent on record.
The analysis, released by WaterAid and carried out by academics at the universities of Bristol and Cardiff, examined 44 years of rainfall in 12 South and South-East Asian cities alongside the strength of past El Niño events, and found that the stronger the El Niño event, the more certain it became that a city's rainfall would swing away from normal.
However, cities swung in opposite extremes, the researchers found, with some pushed towards drought and others, sometimes only a few hundred miles away, pushed towards flooding.
Jakarta and Surabaya in Indonesia; Phnom Penh in Cambodia; Bangkok in Thailand, Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia and Mumbai in India all became drier as El Niño strengthened, with the very strongest events clustering at the driest outcomes in the data.
Meanwhile, Shanghai and Hangzhou in China and Colombo in Sri Lanka went the other way, becoming reliably wetter. Faisalabad and Karachi in Pakistan and Dhaka in Bangladesh sit between the two zones and have swung either way, which makes them the hardest for governments to plan for.
El Niño begins with a warming of the surface of the Pacific and ends up moving moisture around the planet in ways that leave some regions in flood and others in drought, depending on where they sit relative to that movement. It occurs every five to ten years, and its strength is measured by how far sea surface temperatures deviate from normal.
What makes this year different is the scale of the event, which is already being labelled “super” this year. Meteorological agencies and researchers around the world are on high alert that this El Niño has gained strength at an exceptional speed, and could affect every weather pattern.
It could reach as high as 3.6C above normal, against a previous monthly record of 2.75C set during the El Niño of 2015 and 2016. Nothing on record approaches what is forecast, which the researchers say leaves the size of the impact genuinely uncertain.
"Under the unprecedented super El Niño, we are in unchartered territory because there is no event on record as large as what is predicted," the researchers said. "There are definitely uncertainties relating to the magnitude of the impact. However, based on our analysis, there seems to be more certainty related to the direction of the impact. Regions normally prone to drought will highly likely experience drought and regions normally prone to flooding will highly likely experience flooding."
"When we get to territory like a super El Niño, it means that that difference in sea surface temperatures, that anomaly that we're measuring across the globe, is really extreme," said Michael Singer, professor at Cardiff University and one of the lead scientists. "So we're expecting a lot more moisture to be moving around in very specific ways around the planet, leading to in some places, you know, probably really high propensity for flooding, and in other places, a high likelihood of drought."
For the South Asian cities in the drying group, the effect will interrupt a pattern running the other way. WaterAid's earlier research found most of these cities have been getting steadily wetter over four decades, with fewer droughts and more extreme rainfall. A dry spell might sound like relief in a region currently dealing with floods, but Katerina Michaelides, professor at the University of Bristol, said that misreads how long these events last.
"The impacts of an El Niño may last for not just one year or one season. They may be prolonged. They may be a year. They may be two years. They may be multiple seasons of below-normal rainfall back to back, depending on how long the El Niño lasts and the strength of it," she said.
"Unless these places are well equipped to manage and store water from the wet season to use during drought periods, it's never really a good thing to have prolonged drought periods in regions that are used to having a certain amount of seasonal rain come in, where agriculture and livelihoods are tied to a sort of consistent pattern."
A weakening of the monsoon in India or elsewhere that depends on those rains is not necessarily good news, she said, unless those places are equipped to handle a long dry period. Professor Singer added that a less intense monsoon could bring short-term benefit somewhere already flooding badly.
Mumbai falls in the drying zone and should expect drought, Professor Michaelides said, while Dhaka sits in a transition zone and could go either way depending on the atmospheric patterns of the moment.
El Niño is not the only thing shaping rainfall in the region. The researchers point to the Indian Ocean Dipole, the Madden-Julian Oscillation and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation, each of which can amplify El Nino's effect when aligned with it or blunt it when running the other way.
"Rainfall in any one place is shaped by many overlapping climate influences, and El Niño is just one of them," Professor Michaelides said. "But our analysis shows that El Niño's strength is still a strong predictor of whether rainfall is likely to deviate from normal."
The same split shows up in East Africa, where the research found neighbouring cities pulled in opposite directions, with Nairobi and Kampala turning wetter while Addis Ababa dries.
Whichever way a city goes, the consequences run through water. Flooding contaminates supplies and spreads diseases including cholera, while drought empties reservoirs and destroys crops, and both fall hardest on cities where water and sanitation systems are already stretched.
"The chaos of the climate crisis, bringing extreme heat, droughts and floods, has been on our doorsteps for some time now, but this year's super El Niño only puts us more at risk," said Shakeel Hayat, climate change and water, sanitation and hygiene specialist at WaterAid Pakistan. "The data makes clear that some of the world's biggest cities could be left with too much or too little water."
Mr Hayat said water security had become a matter of food, energy, health and economic security, and pointed to rainwater harvesting as a straightforward way of easing pressure on depleted groundwater. "There are solutions, we just need investment," he said.
WaterAid is calling on the British government to make water security, sanitation and hygiene a priority of its G20 presidency next year and at the UN Water Conference this year.
The Independent has previously reported that the super El Niño weather event could see global agricultural output take a $342 billion (£260bn) hit, and pose a critical threat to the world’s 500 million smallholder farmers, new research suggests.
That financial forecast is based on 11 key commodities including grains, oils, coffee, cocoa, dairy and livestock, which have a combined anticipated yield loss of up to 14 per cent during the extreme weather event.
Aid groups are warning that global food crises, which have already been hit hard by plummeting foreign aid flows from wealthy countries, could now worsen further with the super El Niño.

title: Met Office issues multiple thunderstorm warnings as flooding and heavy rain expected
text:
Met Office issues multiple thunderstorm warnings as flooding and heavy rain expected
The forecaster has warned that there may be travel disruption and potential power cuts
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Yellow thunderstorm warnings have been issued across the UK, with the Met Office warning of heavy downpours and flash flooding after weeks of extreme heat.
The warnings are set to come into place later on Wednesday, and cover large swathes of northern England, Northern Ireland and parts of Scotland.
The forecaster has warned that homes and businesses could be flooded and there may be disruption to transport services and power cuts.
It follows what is likely to be the hottest summer on record, with five heatwaves leaving 71.3 per cent of the country in drought.
The yellow weather warnings are set to come into force at noon in Northern Ireland and last until 11.59pm on Wednesday, while parts of northeast Scotland are under the alert from 2pm until 9pm.
Large parts of north of England, covering Manchester, Liverpool and Newcastle upon Tyne, have been issued a warning from 7pm on Wednesday until 10am on Thursday.
The thunderstorm warnings come as parts of the UK were hit by “heavy pulses” of rain early on Wednesday, but forecasters and officials warned downpours this week would not solve the drought overnight.
Met Office data showed up to 23mm of rain fell in parts of central southern Lancashire in the 12 hours to 6am on Wednesday, with up to 13mm recorded in parts of Northern Ireland and between 6-10mm across southwest England.
In an online forecast, Met Office meteorologist Aidan McGivern said Wednesday would be a “very showery day” across the UK, with Northern Ireland and areas in western and central Scotland seeing “frequent showers with heavy downpours, hail and thunder”.
The cooler and wetter conditions come after the UK’s fifth heatwave of the summer, during which the hottest day of the year was recorded in Kew Gardens, London, on Thursday when the temperature reached 38.1C.
The UK is facing increasingly severe weather extremes such as heatwaves, droughts and flooding – with a risk of surface water floods as heavy rain falls on baked dry ground – as a result of climate change, caused mostly by burning fossil fuels for power stations, vehicles, heating buildings and industry.
All of Wales, and nearly three-quarters of England, are in drought as a result of the hot dry conditions.
The Environment Agency and Natural Resources Wales have applied to the English and Welsh governments for a drought order for the River Severn, warning of the impact the conditions are having on the Severn’s habitats and surrounding farmers.
If granted, it would require Severn Trent Water, South Staffordshire Water, Bristol Water and Hafren Dyfrdwy to reduce the amount they abstract from the river by 5 per cent, which they have said will not affect water supplies.
The order would also impose a cap on the amount of water the Canal and River Trust could take for the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal and reduce releases from a reservoir at the river’s headwaters to stretch the amount of available water over a longer period to support fish and other wildlife.
The warnings come after overnight rain which saw Wisley, in Surrey, break its 62-day dry streak, the longest of any area in the UK, with 1.6mm falling in the early hours.

title: Why can rain cause flooding in a drought?
text:
Why can rain cause flooding in a drought?
Heavy showers are expected to hit the UK on Thursday following months of dry weather
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
Heavy rain is forecast to hit drought-stricken areas of the UK this week, sparking fears it could trigger flooding.
While cooler and wetter conditions are welcome after five back-to-back heatwaves bringing widespread drought and hosepipe bans, heavy rain on dry ground can increase the risk of flooding.
The Met Office said that a rainy front will begin to sweep down from Northern Ireland and Scotland towards the south of England and Wales this week, kicking off a wetter week with cooler conditions that are much closer to average for the time of year.
Heavy showers are expected to hit the UK on Thursday, bringing the chance of surface flooding in places where rainfall is particularly intense, it added.
Here, the Independent explores why flooding is a risk following months of dry weather.
What is a flash flood?
According to the Met Office, a flash flood is caused when the underlying ground cannot cope with the amount of rainfall, or drain it away fast enough.
“Roads can become like rivers and if there is a lot of water, it can flood buildings and carry cars away. So, if the rain is falling too fast for the ground or drains to cope, there is a risk of flash flooding,” according to the Met Office.
Why is there a risk of flooding during a drought?
Normally flooding happens when ocean waves come on shore, snow melts too fast, or when dams and river banks break.
But flooding is also common after a drought.
That’s because when there is a lack of rain, triggering drought conditions, the ground becomes very hard and baked dry.
As a result, when heavy showers hit the solid and dry earth rainwater is absorbed at a slower rate, leaving the water to sit and gather on the surface.
Who could be affected by flooding in the UK?
In the UK millions of people are at risk of flooding in both urban and rural areas, according to the Red Cross.
While some people who live in a flood-prone area will have experienced flooding before, scientists warn that climate change is making flooding more frequent.
The Environment Agency says 5.7 million (one in six) properties in England are at risk from flooding, with parts of northern Britain seeing the biggest increases in flood severity in Europe due to climate change.
The Red Cross warns even areas like London can experience flash flooding, and it did so in the summer of 2021.
Because flash floods are unpredictable, it's advised that everyone thinks about the actions they would take to be prepared.

title: One dead as 800mm of rain brings landslides to South Korea days after drought
text:
One dead as 800mm of rain brings landslides to South Korea days after drought
Roads across the region were cut off and flooding along the coast was made worse by high tide
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
One person was killed in a landslide and two others were injured in southern South Korea after nearly 800mm of rain fell in three days on a region that was in drought a week ago.
Geoje, a coastal city near Busan, recorded 782.5mm between midnight on Saturday and 6am on Monday, according to the Korea Meteorological Administration, close to a third more than London receives in an average year.
Nearby Tongyeong had 628.9mm, Sacheon 318mm and Namhae 231.3mm.
The landslide struck an apartment building in the Okpo district of Geoje at about 4.32am on Monday (8.32pm BST on Sunday), burying the ground floor, the National Fire Agency said. Rescue workers pulled three residents out, one of whom later died in hospital. A second person was rescued after being buried by a landslide in Tongyeong shortly after 5am.
Roads across the region were cut, including National Route 33 in Goseong, and flooding along the coast was made worse by high tide. Authorities received more than 20 reports of people trapped by water or debris, about 100 residents of Geoje were being moved out because of the risk of further slides, and rescuers were working to reach 20 people stranded there, the safety ministry said.
Residents were woken repeatedly by emergency alerts through the night.
"Overnight, I heard the loud emergency alert three times on my phone. Every time I was about to fall asleep, another alert came, warning of heavy rain and advising evacuation," a Geoje resident who gave his surname as Jeong told the Korea Herald.
"It was still raining heavily this morning, and I heard that low-lying areas were flooded and in chaos."
Public transport was suspended in parts of Geoje, and the shipbuilders Hanwha Ocean and Samsung Heavy Industries, two of the city's largest employers, told staff to stay at home.
Prime minister Han Seong Sook told the police, firefighters and other agencies to use every available resource to reach people cut off by the water.
"Please make every effort to provide emergency support so that evacuees face no inconvenience, including by operating temporary shelters," she said, adding that officials should also ensure the safety of rescue workers.
South Gyeongsang province received 141.8mm between 1 July and 15 August, 19 per cent of the average for the period, a drought that affected about 5,700 households and 2,100 hectares of farmland, with crops withering in the fields.
Between 80mm and 150mm more rain was forecast for Monday, with heavy rain warnings in force for Geoje, Tongyeong, Sacheon, Namhae and Goseong, and advisories for Gimhae, Yangsan and Changwon.
Yangsan, in the same province, reached 42.5C on 2 August, the highest temperature measured in South Korea since observations began in 1904, in a heatwave the disease control agency has linked to at least 31 deaths nationwide.
In Japan, four people died on Friday and about 7,000 travellers were stranded overnight at Tokyo's Narita airport after more than 360mm of rain fell in 24 hours in Chiba prefecture, where the weather agency issued its highest rain warning for the first time. Weeks earlier, temperatures passed 40C at several locations and three lions died of suspected heatstroke at a Tokyo zoo.

title: Boy, 4, among six dead in Indiana after days of storms and record-setting flooding
text:
Boy, 4, among six dead in Indiana after days of storms and record-setting flooding
The National Weather Service warned that heavy rain and flash flooding were still possible across central areas of the state, including Indianapolis, throughout the day
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
At least six people have died after days of severe storms and widespread flooding in Indiana, where floodwaters on the White River in Indianapolis reached their peak Sunday.
A 4-year-old boy, two men, and three women are among those who have lost their lives since the severe weather began on Aug. 11, according to Liz Woods, a spokesperson for the state Department of Homeland Security.
The city Department of Public Works reported that floodwaters from the White River crested early Sunday morning, with elevated levels anticipated to linger for a few hours prior to beginning to recede.
Emergency shelters remained open as hundreds of homes situated along the river and its canals were evacuated. First responders utilized boats to pull people to safety after they became stranded by rapidly rising water.
The National Weather Service warned that heavy rain and flash flooding were still possible across central areas of the state, including Indianapolis, throughout the day.
Advising residents to check weather and river forecasts, the weather agency urged the public to "stay out of dangerous, fast moving waters" as heavy rain caused major flooding along most rivers and creeks across central Indiana. Forceful torrents also severely damaged or completely washed out bridges and roads across the state.
Approximately 130,000 electricity customers statewide remained without power by midday Sunday, down from a peak of around 300,000, according to Woods and tracking site PowerOutage.us.
Battering Indiana over the past week, heavy rain forced local rivers to crest and set new records.
In Anderson and Noblesville, the White River reached over 24 feet (7.32 meters), surpassing records established back in 1913.
Indianapolis Mayor Joe Hogsett said the city is experiencing its worst inundation in more than 30 years.
Gov. Mike Braun’s office confirmed that emergency crews carried out more than 350 evacuations along with numerous welfare and rescue checks elsewhere in the state, including at a senior mobile home community north of Indianapolis.
President Donald Trump on Saturday granted Braun’s request for federal disaster assistance to aid local response and recovery efforts.
The torrential rainfall and destructive floodwaters were among the impacts of severe storm systems that have wreaked havoc across the Midwest and beyond in recent days.
Tornadoes, heavy rain, and flash floods inflicted widespread damage on communities ranging from Illinois to western Pennsylvania.

Five dead in Indiana as ‘once-in-a-lifetime’ flooding swallows homes - and water ‘is still rising’
Gov. Mike Braun has requested a presidential emergency declaration to secure federal resources following record rainfall

- CommentsGo to comments
At least five people have died in flooding across Indiana this week, state authorities said, as emergency responders worked Saturday to rescue residents from rising waters along the White River in Indianapolis.
The state has suffered heavy rains over the past week, resulting in rivers and creeks overflowing.
Gov. Mike Braun said Saturday that President Donald Trump plans to approve his request for federal assistance to aid response and recovery efforts.
Expressing sympathy for families who lost loved ones, Gov. Braun urged residents to take the flooding seriously and stay clear of floodwaters.
More than 90 people and their pets were rescued Saturday as waters rose along the White River in Indianapolis, with central Indiana authorities responding to historic flooding.
Damage has been concentrated along the river corridor from Hamilton County into the northern Indianapolis suburbs. To the east in Delaware County, sheriff deputies on Friday found the body of a 58-year-old woman believed to have died after trying to drive through floodwaters.
Indianapolis Mayor Joe Hogsett was joined by emergency managers at a briefing Saturday as he urged residents near the river to evacuate. He declared a local emergency a day earlier after heavy rains caused streams to swell.
"This is one of those once-in-a-lifetime type floods," Jacob Spence, director of Marion County Emergency Management, told The Associated Press. "So yeah, this is an unprecedented event and unfortunately we're setting some new records."
Gov. Mike Braun requested a presidential emergency declaration to secure federal resources following record rainfall.
The National Weather Service reported that over 11 inches (28 centimeters) of rain fell within two days in some areas. The White River crested above 24 feet (7.32 meters) in Anderson and Noblesville, breaking records set in 1913.
Flash-flood warnings and watches covered central Indiana on Saturday, with forecasters warning that more showers and thunderstorms would move through the area. In Warren County, 2 inches of rain fell in six hours.
Forecasters expected the White River to crest Saturday evening in Indianapolis, where National Guard vehicles aided rescue efforts. Rita Reith, a spokesperson with the Indianapolis Fire Department, put the total at 91 people and 45 pets rescued by early afternoon.
"The water is still rising, so heed the warnings," said Todd Wilson, director of the city's public works department.
Social media videos showed stranded vehicles, fallen power poles, and flooded intersections.
Earlier this week, severe storms caused damage across the Midwest, bringing tornadoes and flash flooding from the Chicago area to western Pennsylvania.

title: Shocking images show scale of devastation as Assam floods death toll rises to 68
text:
Shocking images show scale of devastation as Assam floods death toll rises to 68
Flooding affects around 700,000 people across dozen districts, submerging more than 800 villages
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
At least 68 people died and more than 700,000 were affected due to floods that inundated hundreds of villages and drove tens of thousands into relief camps across the Indian state of Assam.
Assam, a tea-growing state in India's remote north-east, is crossed by the Brahmaputra, one of Asia's largest rivers, which swells each monsoon and regularly bursts its banks.
This year the flooding has been unusually severe in the state's east, where the death toll rose to 68 by Monday, according to local reports, though official figures issued over the weekend put it at 66. Authorities have warned the number could rise further.
At its peak, the flooding affected around 700,000 people across a dozen districts, submerging more than 800 villages, the Assam State Disaster Management Authority said. By Tuesday the waters had begun to recede and the number of people affected had fallen to about 445,000, according to the news agency PTI.
The district of Sivasagar has been the worst hit, followed by Charaideo and Jorhat, all in the east of the state near the border with Nagaland. Officials have attributed the disaster to a sudden, intense burst of rain, known as a cloudburst, over Nagaland in mid-July, which sent water rushing down into Assam's low-lying plains and overwhelmed rivers already swollen by the monsoon.
The state's chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, described the situation as "very, very pathetic" and said parts of the state had been left in a condition beyond description. He said many residents of Sivasagar and Charaideo were unaccustomed to flooding and had been caught off guard.
"People in Sivasagar and Charaideo are not familiar with floods, and were caught unawares," Mr Sarma said, according to the Assam Tribune.
"The character of the calamity has changed. We need to prepare ourselves for such events in future."
Rescue teams from the army, air force and national and state disaster response forces have been deployed, evacuating stranded residents by boat from areas cut off by the water.
Mr Sarma said road links to some of the worst-affected areas had been severed, leaving tens of thousands of people beyond reach. Efforts to drop supplies by helicopter and drone had failed because the packages burst on landing, he said.
More than 180 relief camps and distribution centres have been set up, sheltering tens of thousands of people. Officials said rice, lentils and salt were being handed out in the worst-hit areas, and power, which had been switched off as a precaution during the floods, was being restored in stages.
The floods have devastated farmland in a state where most people depend on agriculture. More than 35,000 hectares of cropland were left underwater, and hundreds of thousands of cattle and poultry were affected, with thousands swept away. In one village in Sivasagar, a resident, Mitali Gogoi, said her home had been inundated within hours overnight.
"The floodwater inundated our house within hours last night. We didn't even get time to move our belongings," Ms Gogoi told the news agency ANI. "We don't have proper food or drinking water. We collect water from flooded roads in bottles because there is no other option."
Deadly floods return to Assam almost every year during the monsoon, which runs from June to September and brings most of India's annual rainfall.
In 2024 the state's flood season killed more than 100 people and affected millions. Scientists have warned that a warming climate is making such downpours more intense and erratic, while deforestation and building on flood plains leave more people exposed.
The opposition Congress party called for immediate central government assistance for the affected families. Its president, Mallikarjun Kharge, said almost a million people had been affected over the course of the flooding and urged that compensation be provided for every life, home and livelihood lost.

title: Snow in Athens as France burns: Images lay bare contrast in extreme weather across Europe
text:
Snow in Athens while France is on fire: The images that lay bare contrast in extreme weather across Europe
As extreme weather events continue to hit Europe, over 300,000 people have been evacuated amid growing wildfires in Spain and France
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
A series of extreme weather events have battered Europe this summer, leading to vast contrasts in the weather across the continent.
In recent weeks, there has seen snow and severe flooding across Greece, while firefighters continue to battle raging wildfires in France and Spain.
In Greece, an atmospheric shift brought a rare dusting of late-July snow to Mount Olympus.
Athens saw torrential rain bring down utility lines and scaffolding, suspending operations of the capital’s suburban rail network.
The effects of the rain saw 1,000 calls made to emergency services across the country.
Meanwhile, southwestern Europe remains locked in a relentless heatwave, with French and Spanish emergency crews fighting to contain fast-moving wildfires fed by bone-dry terrain and fierce winds.
In France, 2,500 firefighters and 1,500 military personnel have been deployed to the south as flames sweep through the south west region of Gironde, according to the country’s interior minister.
Over 250,000 people have been evacuated, as authorities warn that they could be fighting blazes near Bordeaux for “several weeks or even several months”.
This comes after reports of France’s first “fire cloud” — an extreme weather event that sees the rapid, unpredictable acceleration of wildfires.
The situation is expected to worsen on Tuesday due to a rise in temperatures.
Across the border in Spain, the government has declared a national emergency, as huge fires hit the capital, Madrid, and the nearby province of Ávila, earlier last week.
Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso said has said that it marked the “worst fire in the history of the region.”
Amid mass evacuation orders, the city’s emergency management chief, Carlos Novillo said on Friday that the fire was “currently beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain.”
130,000 hectares of land had been burned in Spain so far this year, according to Spanish Prime Minster, Pedro Sánchez.
This figure is ahead of the country’s annual average of 100,000 hectares scorched by wildfire over the last decade.
At least one man has been killed in Spain and dozens of others have been injured, including at least 68 firefighters in France.
Scientists warn these stark contrasts reflect an increasingly volatile climate system, driving extreme weather events across the continent.

title: Tropical Storm Bertha makes landfall in Louisiana with 45 mph winds
text:
Tropical Storm Bertha makes landfall in Louisiana with 45 mph winds
Authorities issued a tropical storm warning stretching from Alabama to Louisiana
- Bookmark
Tropical Storm Bertha made landfall in southern Louisiana on Wednesday, bringing strong winds and widespread closures across the Gulf Coast. The slow-moving storm, which had already prompted beach closures from the Florida Panhandle to Mississippi, touched down in St. Bernard Parish, approximately 40 miles (65 kilometers) east of New Orleans.
The National Hurricane Center reported Bertha's maximum sustained winds at 45 mph (72 kph) at the time of landfall. Forecasters anticipate the storm will maintain this intensity as it tracks towards the upper Texas coast by Thursday.
Authorities issued a tropical storm warning stretching from Alabama to Louisiana, encompassing New Orleans, where residents were already contending with extreme heat. Parks, piers and some low-lying roads were shut down along the coast as wind and storm surge posed the primary threats to the Deep South states.
By Thursday evening, the storm's center was located about 40 miles (70 kilometers) southwest of New Orleans.
Onlookers watched the storm surge at the Lake Pontchartrain estuary, with kids splashing in the floodwaters as Bertha approached the Louisiana Coast. Residents mowed their lawns even as streets filled up with water.
Tropical storm force winds were felt as much as 160 miles (260 kilometers) from the center of the storm, the National Hurricane Center said. A wind gust of 44 mph (71 kph) was recorded at New Orleans Lakefront Airport on Wednesday afternoon.
The strong gales knocked over a Waffle House sign onto a car in Panama City Beach, Florida.
But the heaviest rains were staying offshore, reducing the risks of flooding, the center said.
The storm is unlikely to leave behind widespread damage, Louisiana State Climatologist Jay Grymes said. The impact should be manageable for coastal communities, he said.
Gov. Jeff Landry called the forecast “encouraging” but also warned residents to be prepared for some flooding.
Storm surges up to 3 feet (1 meter) were possible in Louisiana and Alabama, forecasters said. Rain totals were forecast between 1 and 4 inches (3 to 10 centimeters), with higher amounts possible in isolated areas.
Bertha is expected to dissipate inland in Texas by Friday, the hurricane center said.
Bertha is expected to continue losing strength over the next few days as it heads toward Texas after the storm earlier trudged past the Florida Panhandle and the tips of Alabama and Mississippi. At landfall, the storm's maximum sustained winds were around 45 mph.
Elsewhere in the U.S. this week, a line of storms generated reports of tornadoes stretching from Cincinnati to New Jersey. Torrential rains caused flash floods Tuesday night that swamped homes, washed out bridges and led to water rescues in West Virginia, authorities said.
Sandbag distribution sites are set up
Authorities in Mississippi, Louisiana and Florida opened sites to provide sandbags to residents who may be impacted by Tropical Storm Bertha. Double-red flag warnings were posted along some beaches, closing them to swimmers.
“For locals, this is just another storm,” said Candice Henderson, manager of the Crab Trap, a beachside restaurant that was packed Tuesday on Pensacola, Florida’s Perdido Key. “When you’re on vacation and it's raining, you either shop or you go out to eat.”
Bertha is the second tropical storm of the Atlantic hurricane season. Tropical Storm Arthur in June brought heavy rainfall to the southeastern U.S.
Bertha could dump heavy rain on coastal areas of Mississippi that are still recovering from flooding brought by Arthur that destroyed and damaged homes.
Hurricane Fausto in the Pacific is far from land
In the eastern Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Fausto churned far from land Wednesday. The hurricane was hundreds of miles west-southwest of the southern tip of Baja California with maximum sustained winds of 80 mph (130 kph).
It was forecast to gradually strengthen and the hurricane center warned that ocean swells generated by Fausto could cause life-threatening surf and rip tide conditions on the Baja California coast.

title: Flooding tests Texasâ new warning systems a year after Camp Mystic tragedy
text:
Floods test Texas’ new warning systems a year after Camp Mystic tragedy
Officials in Texas have implemented major changes to improve flood warnings after last year's deadly floods in Hill Country
- Bookmark
Catastrophic flash floods have once again ravaged parts of Texas, claiming at least two lives and prompting hundreds of rescues, just a year after a similar disaster in the Hill Country killed over 100 people.
This new deluge arrives as state officials were still working to implement major changes promised in the wake of last July's tragedy, which included better flood warning systems, tighter safety rules for children's camps, and improvements to water infrastructure.
Despite the ongoing devastation, residents in some of the hardest-hit areas reported that a year of preparation did make a tangible difference. Newly installed flood sirens blared warnings in the darkness, urging people to evacuate, and phones buzzed with critical alerts that were notably absent during last year's disaster.
However, the sight of homes unexpectedly inundated by rising rivers illustrates the formidable challenges of bolstering early warning systems across "Flash Flood Alley," a vast and rural region inherently prone to sudden and severe flooding.
Some agencies were more proactive about sending wireless alerts
Over the last decade, a variety of Texas state and local agencies missed opportunities to implement flood warning systems along the Guadalupe River, the AP reported after last summer’s floods killed 136 people, including 28 at a sleepaway camp for girls.
That changed after the tragedy as lawmakers and others scrutinized a lack of preparedness by government agencies and riverside camps.
Unlike last summer, when local officials in Kerr County said they had been reluctant to “cry wolf” and order evacuations and failed to send out wireless alerts to warn of flash floods, Kerr County issued four alerts and the city of Kerrville issued one early on Thursday as the risk for flooding became apparent, according to an Associated Press review of available data.
They warned residents along Quinlan Creek to evacuate to higher ground, and of “extremely dangerous” flash flooding. Those alerts came alongside flood watches, warnings and emergencies sent to broadcast outlets, weather radios and mobile phones by the National Weather Service. People who signed up for the CodeRED notification emergency system in Kerr County also received text message warnings.
“Last year, we got no alarms. We had no idea what was going on,” said Suzanne Sutphin Gschwind, of Kerrville.
“This year, very different,” she said, with multiple texts and calls coming in from local authorities, a weather channel and her doorbell camera. One night the warnings arrived “about every two hours.”
“I think we would all like to err on the side of too much,” she said.
The warnings didn't reach everyone
Between the early morning hours of Tuesday and about 9 a.m. Thursday, the National Weather Service sent 38 alerts to people in certain southwest Texas communities, including 14 tornado warnings and 24 warnings that flooding was occurring or imminent and could be “life threatening.”
Those Weather Service notifications, though, often don’t contain the highly localized information put in alerts sometimes sent by municipal and county emergency agencies — and people in some places may not have gotten any of those local alerts, which can be more decisive for people considering whether to seek high ground.
An Associated Press review of wireless emergency alert data did not find any listed as sent by agencies in Uvalde County, which was hit hard by flooding, though agencies in that county might have used other means to alert the public.
Jaclyn Gonzales was awakened at 2 a.m. Wednesday by a friend who called to warn that a tornado might be headed toward her Uvalde-area home. When she jumped out of bed, the floor was wet.
“It was the shock of the water to my feet that made me really wake up,” she said.
Kat Sprawls only learned floodwaters were nearing her Batesville home when a friend called her at 3:30 a.m. Friday. It took five or six calls before she woke up, because she had her phone on do-not-disturb mode.
“There's no warning system at all. It's just like the flood in Kerrville last year — we had no warnings,” Sprawls said. “Over half of Batesville is under water now."
Zavala County Sheriff's Department secretary Jessica Belmarez said the department is updating its Facebook page with evacuation information and that law enforcement officers were going door-to-door in affected areas, including Batesville.
The network of flood sirens is expanding
Newly installed sirens in Ingram and in Kerr and Kendall counties were used this week to warn residents, said state Sen. Paul Bettencourt, who authored legislation in 2025 to help fund the sirens. Twenty-eight additional counties are also eligible for flood warning funding. Most are in the process of putting together implementation plans for review by the Texas Water Development Board.
“Between the outdoor sirens, and the cellphone alerts, the response was very positive in getting people out of the way and to higher ground,” Bettencourt said. “It’s an enormous improvement over a year ago.”
Three of six new sirens installed in Kerr County were used to warn people to seek high ground, said Tara Bushnoe, manager of the Upper Guadalupe River Authority. The other three were in areas with only minor flooding, Bushnoe said.
The small town of Comfort had one warning siren for years. The volunteer fire department recently installed two more.
“Some people just don’t want to leave — that’s our problem here,” said Danny Morales, the assistant fire chief. “But we did set them off twice, probably an hour from one to another, just because we had people just lingering, and not wanting to move."
Private companies are working to fill the gaps
Ian Cunningham founded River Sentry after the 2025 floods, building flood siren towers for privately owned sites like RV parks, camps and hotels. The sirens are triggered by rising water levels.
So far, the company has installed 104 sirens along the Guadalupe River, Cunningham said, including several near the site of an RV park where more than three dozen people died in 2025.
“We installed them about three months ago and did not expect them to be used so soon,” Cunningham said.
Hononu, which has developed water-level sensor technology and a real-time data network, received a state contract that will make it easier for agencies to purchase its flood warning technology.
Watch Duty, a fire-tracking app used by millions, expanded earlier this year to help monitor floods.
Officials say the changes saved lives
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott said the lessons of 2025 led to a better emergency response this time.
“Everybody in Texas has been far more prepared to deal with what has happened this year,” Abbott said during a news conference in Uvalde. “Lives have been saved.”

title: LAâs Sunset Boulevard floods after century-old pipe bursts
text:
Century-old pipe bursts flooding famed Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles
The pipe rupture engulfed one of Los Angeles’ busiest corridors in thousands of gallons of water
- Bookmark
- CommentsGo to comments
The rupture of a century-old pipe transformed a stretch of Sunset Boulevard into a rushing river, engulfing one of Los Angeles’ busiest corridors in thousands of gallons of water.
On Thursday morning, a 36‑inch underground pipe burst without warning at the convergence of Sunset and Holloway Drive, opening a sizable sinkhole and sending a torrent coursing down the surrounding streets for several hours.
From above, the scene looked surreal: water cascading along tree‑lined blocks, vehicles stranded in rising currents, a fleet of buses partially submerged and what appeared to be an underground parking garage filled with several feet of water. No injuries have been reported.
Crews worked through the night to drain the sinkhole and excavate a roughly 25‑foot section of the broken main. On Friday, Sunset Boulevard remained closed as repairs continued, and officials urged residents to avoid the area and conserve water.
“We are grateful that no injuries have been reported as a result of this significant water main break,” West Hollywood Mayor John Heilman said in a statement on Thursday. “We know these road closures and traffic impacts are disruptive, and we appreciate everyone's patience as crews work to stabilize the area, assess the damage, and begin repairs.”
The steel pipe, constructed in 1916, ruptured shortly before 4 a.m. Thursday, sending water across the hills of West Hollywood and down its inclined streets.
Area residents woke to find water rushing past their front doors. Dozens of buses were seen submerged under water, and some nearby businesses had sopping wet floors. Firefighters deployed to the area laid sandbags on streets brimming with the overflow.
“For those familiar with this area, you know the topography. It’s a lot of hills, streets with an incline, so that’s creating this massive rush of water,” an ABC7 reporter said on Thursday morning.
The outlet reported that crews managed to stop the flooding around 7 a.m.
“As [Los Angeles Department of Water and Power] crews continue to work urgently to remove water to repair the pipe rupture in West Hollywood, people should avoid the area and conserve water as some may experience a loss of water pressure,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said on Thursday. “Water to the pipe has been shut off, and anyone who has experienced damage should speak to LADWP personnel on the ground…”
On Friday, LADWP said crews remained on scene, working to reshore the compromised infrastructure. A 0.7‑mile section of the main had been drained, with about 195,000 gallons of water removed from the site and a 25‑foot section of the damaged pipe cut out.
Sunset Boulevard between Sherbourne Drive and San Vicente Boulevard is still closed to traffic, with some sidewalks rendered unusable. The ruptured pipeline — installed when Woodrow Wilson was in the White House — had already been slated for replacement.
“While repairs to the damaged 25-foot section are being completed now, LADWP will continue moving forward with the long-term replacement plan,” the agency said.
Despite the break and the dramatic flooding, the agency said its overall leak rate remains 36 percent lower than the national average.

title: At least one dead and over 70 rescued as Texas floods reach deadly levels
text:
At least one dead and over 70 rescued as Texas floods reach deadly levels
A ‘large and deadly flood wave’ is surging down a river that tragically claimed two dozen lives at Camp Mystic just a year ago
- Bookmark
At least one person has died and dozens have been rescued as Texas grapples with intensifying and dangerous flooding after days of relentless rain.
“Our number one focus is saving lives,” Gov. Greg Abbott said Thursday afternoon.
There was “one loss of life” so far, Abbot said, but he did not specify where or when. More than 1,300 personnel were responding and have rescued well over 70 people.
Emergency crews began rescues before dawn while issuing urgent warnings: "Move to higher ground now!"
The National Weather Service in San Antonio has cautioned of a "large and deadly flood wave" surging down a river that tragically claimed two dozen lives at Camp Mystic just a year ago.
The severe weather threatens multiple counties near the Mexican border and across the Texas Hill Country.
Officials in Kerrville advised residents to seek shelter on the highest levels of their homes, while the Uvalde County Office of Emergency Management issued a shelter-in-place order, stating: "All major highways and many city streets are closed due to flooding and water over the roadway."
No immediate reports of deaths or injuries have emerged, though several tornado warnings were also issued.
The weather service reported that 10 to 20 inches of rain have fallen over the past two days, with a staggering 8 inches recorded in just two hours early Thursday.
A gauge less than 10 miles from Kerrville indicated the river had risen 32 feet in a mere four hours, with expectations that it could reach a crest similar to that of the catastrophic July 4, 2025 flood.
Forecasters had warned that perilous conditions were likely to worsen in some hard-hit communities, with the deluge dumping nearly a foot of rain in certain areas.
This latest event comes as parts of the Texas Hill Country are still recovering from last summer’s devastating floods, which resulted in more than 100 fatalities.
Flood watches are anticipated to remain in effect through Friday evening for some regions.
By Wednesday, Uvalde police had initiated mandatory evacuations for specific areas, with first responders directly notifying affected residents. Others were urged to remain vigilant for potential further evacuations.
Residents watched anxiously as the water encroached, with some along the Leona River hastily packing their cars, uncertain of where to go. One individual was seen loading two kayaks into a truck bed, seemingly as a precaution.
Lightning illuminated darkening skies as the typically calm river transformed into a torrent of brown water, creating large rapids and pushing against the town’s high bridge and into neighborhoods by Wednesday afternoon.
In response to the widespread crisis, Texas Governor Greg Abbott has declared disasters for dozens of counties.
As of Wednesday evening, over 6 million Texas residents across 57 counties were under a National Weather Service flood watch, scheduled to continue through early Thursday night. Watches for 34 of these counties are set to expire Friday evening.
Uvalde County has experienced some of the highest rainfall totals, leading to dozens of rescues and ongoing calls for assistance as river levels continue to climb. Highways and roads throughout the region remain impassable due to high water. The county typically receives approximately 23 inches of rain annually, highlighting the extraordinary nature of the current deluge.
